newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore dollar seen heading for two-year low.
newsitem.headline: Singapore dollar seen heading for two-year low.

text.p: The normally unflappable Singapore dollar is set to plumb lows not seen in over two years against the U.S. dollar as the city-state struggles in an export slump and funds flood into the Malaysian ringgit.

Foreign exchange dealers said the Singapore dollar fell to a low of 1.4443 from just below 1.4400 to the U.S. dollar on Thursday after the government announced an unexpected drop in non-oil domestic exports for February.

They said the move put the Singapore dollar, which has weakened steadily since starting the year just shy of 1.4000, firmly on track to 1.4500, a level not seen since February 1995. "The market has been building up for dollar/Sing to test 1.4500 and ringgit/Sing to test 0.5850 for a few months, so we're almost there," said a U.S. bank dealer.

The Singapore dollar was quoted at 1.4438/48 to the U.S. dollar in late Asian trade on Thursday. The ringgit was at a 30-month high of 58.30/36 Singapore cents against 55.37 at the beginning of the year.

The Trade Development Board said Singapore's non-oil domestic exports fell 7.9 percent year-on-year in February. A Reuters survey of 16 economists earlier in the week produced a average forecast of a 1.5 percent rise.

Dealers and analysts said massive fund flows into the higher yielding Malaysian ringgit, backed by the country's positive economic outlook, were the driving force behind the Singapore dollar's weakness against the U.S. dollar.
Daniel Lian, chief strategist, Asian bond and currency, at NatWest Markets, said the market had pushed the ringgit to a level that was technically bullish, helping perpetuate long positions.

"In the past few weeks, we have seen another few yards (billions) of long ringgit positions being added to the market both on the ringgit/sing crosses and versus the U.S. dollar," Lian told Reuters Financial Television.
He said the exchange rate could consolidate around the 58.30/40 region for a while but an eventual push to 60 Singapore cents was likely this year.
Expressions of unconcern by Singapore authorities about their dollar's fall against the U.S. dollar have also contributed to its descent, analysts said.
"The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) did not intervene when we were at 1.4300 and now we have decisively broken into territory that nobody expected dollar/sing to be traded to," Lian said.

P.K. Basu, director of regional macroeconomics at Union Bank of Switzerland, said sluggish export growth, coupled with subdued inflation, had led to a marginal shift in Singapore's unstated policy of maintaining a strong currency against the U.S. dollar.

He said domestic factors as well as the U.S. dollar's strength against the major currencies had led to a "policy response from Singapore authorities aimed at weakening the Sing dollar against the strong U.S. dollar".
But Jacqueline Ong, regional economist at research firm I.D.E.A., said Singapore was unlikely to condone any sustained weakness in its dollar.
"I think 1.4500 is quite overdone because the government still basically favours a long-term uptrend on the Sing dollar to curb imported inflation," Ong said.
